children: Industry leaders highlight rising investment, infrastructure growth and regulatory bottlenecks shaping India’s hospitality expansion

The 10th edition of the BW Hotelier Indian Hospitality Summit & Awards (IHA) opened in New Delhi on Thursday, September 24, bringing together senior hospitality leaders, policymakers, investors and other industry stakeholders for a wide-ranging conversation on where India's hotel investment story goes next. The summit's Gala Night, recognising the industry's top performers, follows on September 25.

At a session titled "Global Perspectives: India's Hospitality Decade: Global Capital, Global Partnerships & Global Confidence," moderated by Ajay R Sharma of Edelweiss Public Alternatives, Singapore, the panel put hard numbers to India's growth trajectory — and an equally hard set of questions about what stands between the country and its next phase of expansion.
A Market On The Cusp

Matthew G Pohlman, Partner & Chair of the Global Hospitality & Leisure Practice at Goodwin Procter (UK) LLP, London, opened by sizing the opportunity. Hotel investment activity in India stood at roughly USD 600 million in 2026, he noted, and is estimated to cross USD 1 billion — a level of growth that draws envy from other parts of the world. The scale of the runway becomes clearer in context: Europe alone recorded USD 22 billion in hotel investment activity in 2025.

Pohlman pointed to public-private infrastructure partnerships — expressways, airlift connecting tier-one to tier-three cities — as visible drivers, citing the new Delhi-Jaipur expressway link, part of the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway, which has cut travel time between the two cities from roughly four-and-a-half hours to about three.

He also credited India's deep bench of local investors: having local partners who can co-invest, build a deal pipeline and provide a strong base of investors, he said, is a compelling proposition for international capital looking to enter India. Beyond the numbers, he pointed to what he called an "unapologetic ambition" running through Indian boardrooms — a quality he said he doesn't encounter in every market he visits.
The Real Bottleneck: Paperwork, Not Ambition

Pressed by Sharma on concrete near-term priorities, Pohlman summed up his approach to capturing the opportunity in three words: "speed, certainty and execution." He then shifted the conversation from physical to "documentary" infrastructure. Land registry clarity — knowing who owns what, and what encumbrances exist — was, in his view, as important as roads and runways in determining how fast capital can move.

He flagged planning permissions, zoning rights, licences and approvals as the real friction points in taking a hotel from acquisition to operation, arguing that development cycles running 18-24 months in many global markets stretch to three, four, even five-plus years in India — a gap that raises costs and execution uncertainty. His prescription paired streamlined approval timelines with greater market transparency through robust, data-driven benchmarking.
Binod Chaudhary's Reality Check

Dr Binod Chaudhary, Chairman of CG Corp Global, offered a more searching assessment. His group's hospitality arm, CG Hospitality — now run day-to-day by his son Rahul Chaudhary — traces its partnership with IHCL/Taj back to 2001, when it invested in the Taj Samudra in Colombo and two Taj properties in the Maldives; that relationship has since grown into one of IHCL's largest global partnerships.

Today CG Hospitality operates around 190 hotels across 12 countries. Separately, its India arm, Concept Hospitality (majority-owned by CG), recently struck a founding deal bringing its Fern-branded hotels — some 115 properties and roughly 8,000 rooms — under Marriott's new Series by Marriott collection brand.

While praising India's airport and rail upgrades, Chaudhary was candid about the gaps: "India has not yet done what it is capable of doing in the wildlife space," he said, adding that the country has "not fully tapped the potential of its oceans" — pointing to Lakshadweep and Andaman as underused assets.

He also flagged Darjeeling's tea-garden circuit as a missed opportunity despite small recent openings there. His sharpest number was on inbound travel: India's foreign tourist arrivals have hovered in the 9-10 million range in recent years, he noted, against Thailand's far larger numbers. Still, he closed on a note of credit rather than criticism: "Hats off to the industry for sustaining tourism despite these challenges."
The Capital-Return Equation

Closing the segment, Sharma reminded the panel that hospitality remains a long-gestation asset class — three to seven years to build before capital returns — making faster approvals and better data even more pressing for investors weighing India against competing markets.
